content: Currently, there are five primary surgical techniques for performing a hysterectomy in cases of benign gynecological conditions. These include abdominal hysterectomy (AH), vaginal hysterectomy (VH), laparoscopic hysterectomy (LH), robotic-assisted hysterectomy (RH), and vaginal natural orifice transluminal endoscopic surgery (V-NOTES). Within the laparoscopic category, there are further distinctions: laparoscopic-assisted vaginal hysterectomy (LAVH), total laparoscopic hysterectomy (TLH), and single-port laparoscopic hysterectomy (SP-LH). The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of these different surgical approaches for women with benign gynecological conditions. A comprehensive search of multiple databases, including Cochrane, MEDLINE, Embase, and others, was conducted up to December 2022. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing clinical outcomes between different surgical techniques were included. The primary outcomes assessed were the time to return to normal activities, patient satisfaction, quality of life, intraoperative visceral injuries, and major long-term complications such as fistulas, chronic pelvic or abdominal pain, urinary or bowel dysfunction, pelvic floor issues, and sexual dysfunction. A total of 63 studies involving 6,811 women were included in the analysis. The quality of evidence for most comparisons was rated as low to moderate, primarily due to poor reporting and imprecision. 1. Vaginal Hysterectomy (VH) vs. Abdominal Hysterectomy (AH): Women undergoing VH likely returned to normal activities faster than those undergoing AH. The mean difference was approximately 11 days earlier for VH (moderate-certainty evidence). For example, if recovery after AH typically takes 42 days, recovery after VH would likely take between 24 and 38 days. There was insufficient evidence to determine differences in other primary outcomes between these two groups. 2. Laparoscopic Hysterectomy (LH) vs. Abdominal Hysterectomy (AH): Women undergoing LH may return to normal activities sooner than those undergoing AH, with a mean difference of about 13 days earlier (low-certainty evidence). For instance, if recovery after AH takes 37 days, recovery after LH would likely take between 22 and 25 days. However, LH was associated with a higher risk of urinary tract injuries, with an odds ratio of 2.16 (moderate-certainty evidence). If the risk of ureter injury during AH is 0.2%, the risk during LH would range from 0.2% to 2%. There was insufficient evidence to determine differences in other primary outcomes. 3. Laparoscopic Hysterectomy (LH) vs. Vaginal Hysterectomy (VH): There was no clear evidence of differences between LH and VH for any of the primary outcomes. Both techniques were associated with low rates of shortand long-term complications. 4. Robotic-Assisted Hysterectomy (RH) vs. Laparoscopic Hysterectomy (LH): None of the included studies reported on patient satisfaction or quality of life. There was insufficient evidence to determine differences in other primary outcomes between RH and LH. 5. Single-Port Laparoscopic Hysterectomy (SP-LH) vs. Laparoscopic Hysterectomy (LH): None of the included studies reported on patient satisfaction, quality of life, or major long-term complications. There was insufficient evidence to determine differences in rates of intraoperative visceral injuries between these two techniques. 6. Total Laparoscopic Hysterectomy (TLH) vs. Laparoscopic-Assisted Vaginal Hysterectomy (LAVH): None of the included studies reported on patient satisfaction or quality of life. There was insufficient evidence to determine differences in rates of intraoperative visceral injuries or major long-term complications. 7. Vaginal Natural Orifice Transluminal Endoscopic Surgery (V-NOTES) vs. Laparoscopic Hysterectomy (LH): There was insufficient evidence to determine differences in rates of bladder injury between these two techniques. Other primary outcomes were not reported. Overall, adverse events were rare across the included studies. The authors concluded that vaginal hysterectomy (VH) is generally superior to abdominal hysterectomy (AH) when technically feasible, as it is associated with faster recovery, fewer wound infections, and shorter hospital stays. When VH is not possible, laparoscopic hysterectomy (LH) offers advantages over AH, including faster recovery, shorter hospital stays, and reduced risks of wound infections, febrile episodes, and transfusions. However, these benefits must be weighed against the increased risk of ureteric injuries and longer operative times associated with LH. When comparing LH to VH, there was no difference in recovery time, but VH was associated with shorter operative times and hospital stays. Robotic-assisted hysterectomy (RH) and V-NOTES require further evaluation, as there is currently insufficient evidence to demonstrate any clear patient benefits over conventional laparoscopic hysterectomy (LH). The authors emphasized that the choice of surgical approach should be individualized, taking into account the relative benefits and risks, as well as the patient’s preferences. Surgical expertise, which is difficult to quantify and poorly reported in the available studies, may also significantly influence outcomes. In summary, when VH is not feasible, LH offers several advantages over AH, albeit with a higher risk of ureteric injuries. Evidence for RH and V-NOTES remains limited.
